Talk of the town this weekend is Anthropic's "Pacing the Frontier" letter.

Safety might be a genuine concern, but I also think it's a business decision. Assorted leaks indicate Anthropic and OpenAI have a 70%+ gross margin on inference (wildly profitable), most of which they spend on R&D to train new models. Without training costs, the labs instantly become cash cows. A mutually agreed "pacing" of new releases would help them space out training R&D, providing an immediate boost to earnings, which is especially important as they gear up to go public.

If you remember back to when Kimi and Qwen came out with new previews, many Twitter users would lampoon the models for commonly answering they were made by Anthropic or OpenAI. Anthropic's Thursday report on Cyber Security now confirms hundreds of Millions of messages were routed by the Chinese Labs to American models to harvest the responses and data, ultimately letting the Chinese labs distill the model's capabilities.

It feels like many of the AI guys like Sam Altman and Dario Amodei have a "houlier than thou" persona, but I certainly don't think they are stupid. If anything, I think this "safety" posturing is a shrewd way to increase profits and make their businesses more sustainable, going slower is actually more profitable if everyone agrees to comply. The last thing American labs want to do is invest Billions in R&D just for the Chinese labs to release something competitive at 10% of the price just a few weeks later, and I think this safety posturing is actually a shift to "Private Releases", which protect their IP and reduce training costs.

Right now, a $200 Claude plan costs the same for everyone, but its value to everyone is significantly different. Biotech capabilities are worth way more to a Drug Research, cybersecurity permissions are worth vastly more to a Digital Forensics firm. A perfect way to enable price discrimination would be to stop model releases to the general public (while still making progress), and selectively releasing specific capabilities to trusted companies who are willing to pay a premium for cutting edge technology. Coming out and saying that would be vastly unpopular, but doing it "in the name of safety" has much better optics, doesn't it?

Of course, the AI bears seem to be jumping on this as "proof" the cycle is about to burst and are not considering the profit motive at all. Tomorrow they'll probably be right in the short-term with a big move down. Do I think the AI boom is over? No. Even if every AI lab paused advancements, I still think current AI models are so capable they will slowly take over sectors like customer service, basic accounting, web development, etc. Less than 10% of Americans have ever used Claude, and I think what is holding AI back in terms of use in the corporate world is simply implementation and a lack of computing power, not the models themselves.

If markets swoon tomorrow, two names I am looking to add are IES Holdings at $300, and Western Digital at $400.

Ironically, I think Western Digital (and Seagate) are massive beneficiaries of "AI Compliance and Security" even though they may sell off on this news. Generative AI is creating vast amounts of data, both Seagate and Western Digital expect 25% annual growth in exabyte shipments over the next decade, and in the last two quarters pricing has increased 5% a quarter. WDC might look optically expensive at 22x forward earnings, but I believe it has a decent shot at getting up to $39 in EPS within the next two years as 25% volume growth and 10-15% pricing growth continues, placing it under 10x earnings by 2029. As regulatory scrutiny and corporate use of AI increases, safety measures and data retention policies will only drive up further demand for storage. WDC's appearance at the Citi Conference last week hinted at surging demand: "Customers are asking to sign LTAs all the way till 2030 and 2031. We haven't signed them yet, but that's the visibility that we have, again, being a strategic component and having earned that seat at the table." My point is, Hard Drives rarely get mentioned in the context of AI as everyone is focused on Memory, Flash, and GPUs, but as compliance and regulatory requirements increase, the amount of data needing to be retained could explode even higher than the 25% pace everyone is expecting. At a sub-market P/E and nearly 100% payout ratio with highly disciplined supply, I think WDC is actually a value setup masquerading as a high P/E growth name for now.

I also have orders to add to IES Holdings near $300. Regardless of whether frontier labs "pace" development, I believe demand for data centers and computing power is insatiable, and IES represents a capital light way to get exposure alongside a highly aligned management team. Unlike less technical infrastructure names like Sterling Infrastructure (permitting, pouring concrete, site prep), IES is working hard to make itself indispensable to the AI buildout. The continual shortage of electricians makes IES's workforce an even more valuable asset, and IES's continual acquisitions of peers at sub-market multiple (most recently DBM Global at 11x earnings), and their purchases of supply chain components like engine manufacturing and custom steel fabrication (so they can not only install parts but also produce them) leaves IES poised to become an even larger name in AI Infrastructure. IES's larger and more well known peer, Quanta Services, trades at 38x forward earnings, which makes IES's current valuation at a sub-market multiple even more interesting. I like being disciplined on my buys and IES is already a large position for me, but at $300, I will happily add another slug.

Spent some time this weekend using ChatGpt's latest Astra model. What really surprised me was the efficiency of the "computer use" tool.

For a while "Computer Use" and "Agentic AI" has been a gimmick for most, but we are rapidly seeing AI become better at utilizing software, purchasing items, making reservations, etc. The OpenAI complex of names, Oracle and Softbank are rallying hard after the model release, but I'm thinking a bit more of second order effects.

If AI can easily check hotel prices or airfares across dozens of travel websites without getting tired, what does this mean for someone like Booking, Tripcom, Expedia, who hope you don't actually find the cheapest price somewhere else? If people can use AI to input data into Turbotax (Intuit) or create graphics with Adobe, does AI become more of a value add than the software itself? I think these are some interesting questions and that over the next few days, we'll see the market's reaction. I'm not saying computer use is blanket bad for software, but I do think it'll make people question what adds more value.

Hello Group's domestic China business is declining around 20% a year, and they are attempting to offset the atrophy by growing their International portfolio of apps. The allure of MOMO is that, unlike most China names, even as a melting ice-cube it maintains a 100% payout ratio. The company pays a roughly 5% dividend, and also repurchases 10% of shares a year. The repurchases are accretive given the stock trades way below book value of $9, its net cash balance ($6), and around 8x earnings. During Q2 of 2025, MOMO repurchased 1.1 Million shares, for Q2 of 2026 I am anticipating elevated repurchases of around 3 Million shares, and earnings around $0.20, a little lower than consensus of $0.24. Going into earnings I think the setup is pretty balanced, on one hand MOMO will almost assuredly report a slower quarter than consensus, but on the other hand its already trading below net cash with a 100% payout ratio. I think options on both sides here are pretty underpriced. I currently hold MOMO at 2% weight, and have January 2027 4.74 Puts for 0.15 and January 2028 3.74 Puts for 0.15 to protect the position. I like this options structure, MOMO is a turnaround story and the right-tail (growth turnaround) and left-tail (huge slowing of the China business and an elimination of capital returns) are both possible outcomes. By owning Jan 2028 3.74 Puts for 0.15, you are essentially paying 2.8% of the current price to protect downside below 66% of the current price for the next 16 months, and with January 2027 4.74 Puts you're paying 2% of the current price to limit near-term downside to 15%, both seem relatively inexpensive given Chinese ADR's propensity to fall apart.

I think downside protection for China names is a must, I like paring the 2% stock position with January 2027 4.74 and January 2028 3.74 Puts. This provides enough time to see if the turnaround happens, while also capping avoiding "burn" risk if things really head south.

Major updates from Hynix and the US Treasury

Hynix - Hynix announced a 40 Trillion Won Buyback program earlier this morning. The buyback is set to commence immediately and execute until November 19. Importantly, Korea buybacks have daily execution reports, so tomorrow morning we should be able to verify the buyback's execution. More importantly, Hynix changed a line in its Capital Allocation initiative from returning "up to 50% of Free Cash Flow" to "at least 50% of Free Cash Flow". Ultimately, I think a variable dividend paired with a share buyback program is the most likely outcome, but this announcement should calm market fears of Hynix going off the deep end and doing something silly with the cash, and the sizeable repurchases should help stabilize the stock. I think it is likely Hynix announces a fresh buyback in November, and eventually engages in arbitrage by issuing more shares in the US at a 30% premium, and buying them back in Korea. Either way, last nights announcement was a welcome development, Korean shareholders (as well as US Institutions) were getting increasingly antsy Hynix would exemplify the "Korea Discount" by doing something extremely stupid. By committing to return 50% or more of Free Cash Flow up until the end of 2027, Hynix has put those fears (at least with regard to shareholder returns) to rest. I'm not sure how they stock will entirely react, but I do thing this may "wrongfoot" a lot of traders - many people, particularly in Korea, threw in the towel and gave up on Hynix. This might serve as the catalyst for them to get back in again.

The US Treasury is also stepping in to help the bond market. The US Treasury will be increasing the size of its buybacks of longer-dated US Government Debt from $2 Billion to $4 Billion per operation. It's not quite yield curve control just yet, but these buybacks will similarly increase liquidity and reduce volatility, aiding the longer end of the yield curve.

Special Fixed Income Trade - 9% From Citigroup Notes

Citigroup has an outstanding note, the 2040 7.875% Fixed to Floating Trups - C PRN on IBKR, currently paying a yield of 9%. The notes used to trade at a big premium to par value of $25 due to an accounting quirk - during the financial crisis Citigroup was able to treat the notes as equity instead of debt, and also recorded them on the balance sheet at just 65% of par value. What this meant is that calling the notes early would lead to a pre-tax loss (difference between recorded value and par value), and also reduce Citi's regulatory capital ratios, impacting their ability to repurchase stock. As a result, C-N typically traded at $28 - $29 (implying a 7% yield) as everyone assumed it would not be called away and wanted to pay extra for a higher yield.

Recently, Barrons and Bloomberg published articles saying Citigroup is now pondering taking the capital hit and calling the notes early, and C-N has sold off on significant volume to $26.10 on heavy volume. At this level, I think a compelling risk to reward has presented itself.

At current interest rates, each quarter C-N is paying around 64 cents, and there is also 9 cents of accrued interest on the notes. Furthermore, the notes come with a 30-day notice, meaning that if Citi wants to call the notes they have to give notice 30 days ahead of time, meaning that you'd receive another 20 cents of interest. As a result, at a price of $26.10, your max loss in the event of an early call is $1.10 ($26.10 - $25 call value), less 29 cents in interest, so roughly 81 cents or 3.5% of the initial investment.

I've added it a 1% weight and placed it into my ROTH. The bet here is simple, each quarter Citigroup kicks the can down the road and doesn't call the notes we collect 65 cents, in two quarters, that's breakeven, and everything after that represents a 9% yield from Citigroup, which I find highly attractive. If Citi does indeed call the notes in the next month, the loss is just 3.5%, not that bad. Interest is normally taxed at ordinary income rates (37%), but by placing the trade in my Roth the 9% yield is entirely tax free - just need Citi to not call the notes by the end of the year for the trade to break even, and even if they do, the approximately 3% loss is palatable. Given the prospect of an early call, I don't want to pay much more than $26.25 on C-N, but I think the $26 - $26.25 range represents an attractive risk-to-reward with an < 6 months breakeven, fixed income is never really a home run, but I think this trade is worth considering if you are looking for some yield and ok with a potential 3% loss if they call the notes early.

Entravision is set to report earnings after the close today. The stock is up 226% since the feature in the March 2026 Portfolio review, and I am looking to protect profits. I trimmed the position by 21%, and used some of the profits to purchase August 10 Strike Puts on the remainder of the position for a cost of 70 cents. No doubt it's an expensive hedge (almost 6% of the current price to hedge downside past a -12% move) but after making several large mistakes with Western Digital and Kioxia, I want to avoid making the same mistake again.

One of the reason I put on the hedge is I believe earnings today are a total wildcard and that options are underpriced in both directions. Last quarter, Entravision's ad-tech business Smadex grew 75% quarter-over-quarter (and some of the growth was contributed by a single customer). People on the more conservative side, such as myself, aren't looking for much growth at all this quarter - after all, 75% growth is more than acceptable for year-over-year, can you confidently say you expect another 75% quarter of growth? I think not.

On the other, we can play the what if game. If Entravision can stun everyone by reporting another consecutive quarter of growth or paint a rosy outlook on the earnings call, there's no doubt the market might run with the narrative. As a result, I think the opportunity for a huge narrative reset (growth surprising to the upside), or a major slowdown in Smadex, are equally possible. Another quarter of 75% growth could imply $15 - $20, but a sharp contraction back to last-years levels could imply $7 - $9. As a result, I wanted to leave upside remaining on the trade (which is why I didn't collar), and paying 75 cents to ensure the trade is still a 180% winner if things go wrong made sense to me.

It's extremely difficult to estimate earnings here since there are so many moving variables - Smadex growth, the prospect of the sale of specutrum or Entravision's traditional media assets. I'm still in the trade, but wanted to take some profits here and use a portion of the proceeds to protect downside below $10.

"We can currently quantify memory availability and customer willingness to invest at elevated price levels. More earnings out, updates on the WDC, OSB, IFOS, ACIC trades:

WDC - Western Digital came in at $3.56, significantly higher than the $3.31 consensus and the $3.25 midpoint guide. Revenue beat by 2% (up 12% from the first quarter) and margins came in at 54%, significantly higher than the 51% estimate. Despite the beat, the stock is down significantly as exabyte shipment volume came in at 231 Million (vs 239 Million estimate), growth of 23% YOY (below the 25% estimate). I believe a big chunk of the move today is the "whisper" number and overpositioning - subsequent to STX's beat, people piled into WDC and the consensus estimate trended higher. Eveveryone wanted a monster beat which created a difficult backdrop. When WDC's results came in where people expected, it was actually seen as a disappointment.

WDC is about a third of my Memory and Storage basket (12% total), and I remain as convicted to it. The bear case is evident: people are worried WDC will fall behind STX's technology, or that the NAND market will crash, making HDD's less relatively attractive. I understand these concerns, but I don't think they will happen. My thesis for WDC is simple: demand for storage is accelerating at 25 - 30% a year, the market is undersupplied, and alternative storage like NAND is highly priced in relative terms. WDC's average selling price per TB was $16.20, in comparison, the HDD spot market is exchanging hands at $35 - $45 a TB, and NVME storage is currently $250 a TB and expected to jump another 50% by 2027 Q2. My point is simple: Hard Drives remain the only affordable method for long-term data storage, and as long as WDC and STX keep supply stable, we can see pricing jump from $16 a TB to perhaps $30-35 a TB by this time next year.

WDC's guide seemed to spook investors, Gross Margin of 55-56% against this quarter's 54.4% seems like a deceleration, and EPS of $3.85 to $4.15 represents an increase of $0.44 at the midpoint. Frankly, I the quarter was more of a messaging issue, they overguided exabyte growth last quarter, and then this quarter they lowballed everything to create a good backdrop for next quarter. Worthwhile to note they came in 30 cents higher than this quarters midpoint guide, and 3% higher on margin, and I expect they will do something similar next quarter.

Pre-market, WDC is trading at $440, roughly 27.5x annualized Q3 earnings, and 16x 2027 earnings. I continue to think WDC will beat and raise, when you look at pure-play cloud storage names such as Backblaze who are soaring higher, there almost seems to be an element of panic among hyperscalers about having sufficient storage for customer data. The data has to go somewhere, and the most economic option is Hard Drives.

As mentioned in the Portfolio review, I've been short January 520, 560, and 660 covered calls against my position. OSB - OSB reported earnings of 39p vs the 38p estimate and credit quality was solid. The market is heavily penalizing OSB as deposit cost pressures continue to dampen net interest margin, which has been guided down from 225 bps to 215-220 for the remainder of the year. After trimming half my OSB at 550 in the last Portfolio review, I will be adding it back over the next couple of days near 500. I prefer deposit cost pressures to credit concerns, unlike credit issues (which can make names uninvestable) temporary deposit cost pressures can be worked out over time, and I think 0.85x Tangible Book with a 7% dividend yield at 7x earnings is once again an attractive entry point. The 490 - 500 level is also where OSB was previously emptying the clip in terms of repurchases, I expect them to support the stock below 500 via repurchasing 0.05% - 0.1% of the float a day.

IFOS - Difficult quarter for Itafos with a 3 cent loss. Higher input prices continue to pressure margins as Hormuz blocks the shipment of Sulphuric Acid. Itafos is the largest percentagewise loser for me YTD, I round tripped from a 50% gain to a 30% loss, and am very unhappy about how I handled it. Itafos is now a special situation, phopshate fertilizer producers such as Mosaic and Itafos are losing money, and the larger producers such as Mosaic are curtailing supply until pricing improves. What this means is it will take a bit more time for Itafos to get back to break even, and until it does, I think the stock is likely to trade poorly. I'm still holding my position as I think once the situation resolves the re-rate will be rapid, but until then I'm bumping it down to a low conviction trade - I don't have hope for reversion anytime soon.

ACIC (Short) - At first glance ACIC looks like it met expectations, but I think the numbers are worse when you look closer. GAAP EPS of $0.44 was padded by a $4.2 Million gain on equity securities, once you strip that out Core Income was closer to $0.33 a share, pretty bad relative to last year's $0.54. Gross Premiums earned were down 16% YOY, and Net Premiums earned were down 11% YOY, showing exactly what I had been concerned about in the FL market: commercial insurance is getting extremely competitive and rates are plummeting. ACIC lowered the revenue forecast to $300 - $320 Million from the previous $335 - $365 Million guidance, and I think 2027 will be an even more challenging year as the Commercial Insurance market deteriorates. The short position is currently up 3% from the $11.20 entry and I have it at -1% weight, on any bounce above $11 I plan on adding another 50 bps of exposure. Unlike IGI who posted 19% YOY growth in Net Written Premium, I think it's clear that ACIC is on defense, and I don't expect value names on defense to ever attain a meaningful premium above book.

A little more commentary on the IGI call. War related losses in the first half were $39 Million, roughly 90 cents a share. Earnings would've been $1.80+ without, but that's ok. India business is rapidly picking up, and IGI has seen no significant war related losses so far in Q3 (most of the dent was caused in March / April). Think IGI is well on its way to 70 cents + in earnings for Q3 provided things stay quiet, and furthermore, improving Long Tail, growing Political Violence demand, and IGI's India business should provide a nice tailwind. Remains to be seen how large the India opportunity is, the way it was described on the call was that "they were just setting up the office in GIFT City and had a few employees in the office", yet business ramped up to $8 Million by the end of Q2. Whether this pace will continue in Q3 is uncertain, but if it does, should mark a new era of expansion for IGI - I think in the past, IGI has managed expectations well, and that perhaps they were lowballing the opportunity on this call to leave an upside surprise later this year driven by India. Overall, I think IGI is back on track for $3 in annualized earnings, and that the stock should trade at 10x earnings, implying upside to $30 a share. The company seems to aggressively repurchase shares on any dip to $25, so I think downside is relatively contained and that over time, IGI will continue to handily outperform the broader insurance industry.

Additionally, WDC reports later today. The consensus of $3.31 is well within range, I am looking for $3.40 - $3.50, and think WDC needs to hit those levels for results to be deemed ok. I still like WDC almost as much, if not more, than the Memory trade, because I think it is unlikely to be disrupted. There is minimal prospect of Chinese supply, and furthermore, optimizations to Storage have already been well discovered, and there is simply a limit to how much you can compress data. As the world's storage needs grow and as AI creates record amounts of data, I believe Hard Drives represent the economical solution to data storage. The reason I prefer Western Digital to Seagate is because of Western Digital's aggressive capital allocation. They are rapidly repurchasing shares, and I am hopeful that on the call they confirm 80% of earnings, if not more, are going to be used for share repurchases. The consensus estimate for 2027 earnings is $23, I am much closer to $25 - $30 and think Western Digital is within striking distance of $40 in 2028, which implies the stock is trading at less than 14x 2028, not that expensive for a very rational duopoly.

The Long-Tail and Reinsurance segments appear to be in growth mode, and I think IGI also has significant opportunity to grow its Specialty Short-Tail segment, in particular Marine and Political Violence. Hyundai Green Food - Hyundai Green Food reported record EPS of 942 Won, growth of 30% from the previous year. Operating leverage continues to improve, and unlike most Korean value names, Hyundai Green Food is actively returning capital to shareholders. Roughly 2% of shares were cancelled in the quarter, and the company has capacity for another 1% (roughly 300,000 shares) until November. I continue to think the blend of a nearly 3% dividend yield, significant share repurchase activity, upside to book, and the stable nature of Hyundai Green Food's business makes it a highly attractive value opportunity. I continue to like Hyundai Green Food and iM Financial the most within the Korean value basket, unlike Hy-Lok (who I still like), Hyundai Green Food and iM Financial are consistently repurchasing shares at 5.5x - 6.0x earnings, which is highly accretive to future earnings, stabilizes the stock, and ultimately I think both have a chance to trade at 8x - 9x earnings over the next several years, which implies 40% upside from the current price.

IGI - It's really difficult to estimate IGI earnings this quarter. Naturally, there is a significant headwind of one-time losses from recent events in the Middle East. A $20 Million loss could be as much as 40 cents, the consensus estimate is 60 cents and I am forecasting something in the 20 - 40 cent range. In terms of capital management, it is clear from past repurchase activity (and the chart) that IGI is ferocious in repurchasing shares in the 24 - 25 range. Given the stock was only in this range for a few days in the quarter, I am estimating 120,000 shares repurchased, a step down from last quarter's 500,000, but simply a result of the stock bouncing from the lows.

Despite lower repurchase activity and the earnings impact from Middle East volatility, I think the important thing to pay attention to is IGI's commentary on Political Violence, Marine, and Energy pricing. Historically, difficult events for insurance have spelled opportunity for IGI - when larger names get hit, IGI swoops in to gain market share and underwrite at highly attractive rates. If you take a look at their expansion into the US, or their foothold in insurance, it was prompted by significant volatility that caused other, larger competitors losses, that ultimately drove them away. From the brokerage commentary I have seen, Political Violence (and to a lesser extend Energy) insurance is up 1,000% - 5,000% in the Middle East since the war broke out. Many larger insurers have taken significant losses, customers are clammoring for coverage, and the companies with minimal expertise are unwilling to have exposure. As a result, Middle Eastern experts such as IGI are potentially seeing a flurry of new business, and they know how to price it favorably. Even if a quick peace deal with Iran is reached, it is likely insurance rates remain sky high as attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure leave a lasting impact. In fact, a peace deal would actually be beneficial as it would reduce the prospect of future losses, while insurance rates would still remain high. As a result, for IGI, I'm not expecting a beat at all, but I think the important thing to pay attention to is their commentary on Middle East pricing, and furthermore, if they have the capacity and expertise to underwrite.

Broader indexes were relatively flat this week, but I think the market sent a big message on the AI trade that wasn't necessarily bullish for the Memory makers (despite the 20% Thursday rally). For the past several months we have seen hundreds of traders become extremely bearish (and in fact, launch careers) out of saying the Hyperscalers are making a mistake and that ROIC on capex is unattractive. This week, Microsoft and Amazon significantly refuted their points and posted the largest 1-day moves in decades, Microsoft is set to extend the useful life for data centers from 15-25 years, and Amazon is indicating the shortage of compute is severe and will easily last into 2028. Both seem to be banging the drum that their capex is a result of the opportunity they see. Despite this bullishness, the memory names were especially weak on Friday.

I'm a big bull on AI, and I think most of you would agree the convenience and information it conveys far exceeds the cost. Given the total shortage of available GPUs, it seems insatiable demand from businesses indicates this as well. Programming, data entry, photo classification, the automation opportunities are endless and I believe AI will bring about a sharp increase in productivity in the coming years. The question is, as AI gets bigger, who does the value go to? 

Right now, leading labs like Anthropic and OpenAI are selling inference at 80% margins, running on GPUs sold at 75% margins, using memory sold at 85% margins.

My point is, there is tremendous value to the end user (businesses and consumers), and with margins like these it is clear the middlemen and hyperscalers are making tremendous amounts of money. The question the market seems to be struggling with is "In 5 years who will be getting the value that is created". Personally, I am not sure if it will be the frontier labs (Kimi has near-frontier performance at a fraction of the cost), and the market itself seems to be clearing doubting Hynix and Samsung given they trade at under 5x earnings. The consensus view seems to be rapidly shifting towards "The hyperscalers can earning a high 20s low 30s ROIC on capex, and if for whatever reason the Memory and Storage bubble bursts in 2028, their profit margins will only grow". That line of thinking does make sense to me, if someone is getting $50 - $100 in value each hour from renting a GPU for $10 and memory gets cheaper, will Google hurry to slash prices or will customers demand more favorable long-term contracts? Probably not.

Right now, Hynix, Micron, and Samsung are selling memory at prices more than 300% higher than where they were last summer, and I think the market is pricing in the possibility  that Hynix and Samsung's $600 Billion expansion plans implode pricing by 2028. The problem with these fears (along with China supply fears) is that they can't be dispelled easily, it's almost up to Hynix and Samsung to "prove" these fears wrong, and that will take time. As a result, I'm not expecting an immediate re-rate for the Memory trade back to June highs, and if anything, I put on the EWY + 160 Put - 150 Put - 200 Call for August trade to get some close-range protection in exchange for giving away all my upside above another 25% move. Another thing that alarms me about Memory is that there are a lot of signs of cultishness, earlier this week there was a rumor Nvidia's next generation GPUs might ship with 192 GB of HBM instead of 384 GB of HBM, whether or not this is true, the memory bulls had an immediate violent reaction, which I think indicates defensiveness and overpositioning. If you remember back to November and December, the Memory bears were defensive, cultish, and opining "price to book", unfortunately it now seems that the roles have reversed, and until there is some clarity about the Memory trade or indication of shareholder friendly capital allocation from Samsung and Hynix, I'm not in a mood to buy or sell, and I do think upside is relatively limited.

The other main component in the Memory and Storage basket is Western Digital, and I am not that worried about AI jitters in terms of Hard Drives. Not only is data creation and storage demand skyrocketing, the price of alternative storage from NAND is growing evening faster and the two largest Hard Drive makers (Western Digital and Seagate) have essentially admitted supply fixing in public. While Western Digital looks incredibly expensive at 54x trailing earnings, I think record storage demand and consistently improving pricing has them on track for $25 in EPS in 2027 with minimal capital expenditure and the ability to return 90%+ of free cash flow via share buybacks. Even if NAND pricing slows in 2027 and is flat in 2028, it will still be several multiples higher than Hard Drives - I think this means demand for Hard Drives will continue to grow uninterrupted while supply remains extremely tight, and controlled by two rational actors (plus Toshiba, who has much smaller market share and relatively limited supply). As a result, I think under $500 represents an interesting entry point for some $WDC exposure, it isn't optically cheap like Hynix or Samsung Preferred, but I believe the trade is less likely to be disrupted. As for the broader market, still sitting on 25% cash and waiting for new, compelling opportunities to present themselves.

While these machines won't have an immediate effect on global semiconductors, they do poise a threat in a few years.

For several years, China's semiconductor industry has been plagued by a lack of efficient tooling due to US export bans on crucial semiconductor equipment. As a result of this blockade, China's DRAM production has been low-grade, yields have trailed peers, and they simply haven't been a legitimate competitor. There is no data out yet as to the effectiveness of China's new DUV machines, but if they can self-source these critical machines, within the next decade they may be able to significantly ramp up memory and semiconductor production in a much more efficient manner. I'm not saying they will be on par with global manufacturers, but even the small prospect that they could should  discount valuations. Even if you are the most bullish memory guy out there, I think it is easy to understand how these developments solidify the left-tail bear case.

I also wanted to discuss some recent updates within AI. On Friday, Moonshot AI (leading Chinese lab) released an Open Source Model named Kimi 3. I have tried it, and the performance is excellent. Industry observers say it is a bit below Fable 5, but what is really impressive is the fact Kimi is so powerful amidst US export restrictions on chips, and furthermore, its innovative memory technology. For those of you who don't know, AI models (within inference) utilize memory for two main functions, holding the model itself (weights), and the KV cache (scratchpad). Kimi uses something highly innovative called Kimi Delta Attention, which is able to maintain performance while heavily reducing KV cache usage for higher context messages, an architecture different from Turboquant. Will this crush demand for memory? Probably not. If anything, cheaper AI might increase inference demand. But I do think Chinese model's innovations, and the fact they are 6-12 months behind US labs and provide excellent performance at a fraction of the price, is ultimately bad news for Frontier Level labs. Whether China cheated and "distilled" US model data to create these models or not, I think the fact Kimi will soon be releasing this model for free represents a challenge to Frontiers who offer their models via API at a very high margin, and it may in fact spook investors from providing further capital.

Whenever I look at short-term price action, I try to see which side is "coping", and despite the compelling fundamentals of Memory and NAND, reactions to new developments seem increasingly "defensive", which I think is a sign people are overextended and that a further move down could snowball into a nasty meltdown. As a result, despite the Memory and Storage basket (Western Digital, Hynix, Samsung Preferred, and Kioxia) falling from 22.5% to 15% weight in my Portfolio from sheer price declines, I am not adding to any of the names until I see things stabilize - catching a falling knife is increasingly difficult, and I think you can probably do better by preserving capital and cash and waiting until things settle down.

Morning gents. As discussed previously, I capped the memory and storage basket to 17.5%, but after the move down the past two days the basket weight has fallen to 15% so I've begun covering some of my DRAM short to bring it back to the 17.5 - 20% range.

Before we get into the bull case, I think it makes sense to understand what the bears are thinking. First of all, from a technical aspect, a lot of the Retail speculators are max long memory (not a good sign) and 2X SK Hynix ETF accounts for nearly 20% of Hynix's daily volume. This dissuades a lot of the "contrarian" bears, they also believe that memory prices are bound to blow up the hyperscalers or that memory capacity will soon outstrip demand, leading to a rapid decline in pricing.

I never say never: it's possible they are right. Samsung and Hynix are lining up nearly $500 Billion in spending to bring further capacity online around 2030, and just like how everyone misjudged demand in 2024 and 2025, it is possible they suddenly oversupply. However, for the bears to be right, I think everyone else needs to be exceedingly stupid.

Google, an excellent capital allocator (huge repurchases in the $160s - $180's) is now raising debt and equity to finance a further buildout - would they do that if they didn't see demand? Nebius, a leading hyperscaler, is entirely sold out and is rushing to bring on additional capacity - would they do that if they didn't see demand? Anthropic's ARR is rumored to have surged from $9 Billion at the end of 2025 to $60 Billion in June - would revenue be surging it tokens were worthless?

Of course, we will see countless stories about how one company overspent on tokens, or an AI glitch for someone else, but ultimately, I think we are still at the beginning of an AI cycle that will soon be present in every facet of our lives. Even the bear's stories about YMTC and CXMT don't make much sense to me - China has a history of command-and-control where they force companies to supply state owned enterprises at sub-global margins, if they are going to finance a $300 Billion National Data Center fund, I suspect they will demand Chinese suppliers sell at "reasonable" prices, siphoning this from global supply.

Ultimately, Hynix and Samsung (with their buildout plan) are trying to thread the needle. They can't keep doubling memory prices, and their goal seems to be to take advantage of the widening supply and demand differential to bring on incremental supply while keeping price increases reasonable. As of today, Hynix is trading at 6x forward earnings, and Samsung Preferred at 4x earnings. Samsung Preferred and Hynix remain my favorites within the basket, and I think despite the overwhelmingly bearish sentiment, the Hynix ADR (July 10th) should be bullish for both, and that while memory will be extremely volatile the next several months, it's still worth having exposure to. The only real threat I see to the memory and storage names is some type of stunning technological advancement (imagine Turboquant but even more powerful) that enables AI Models to operate with very little memory. Most AI labs already implement compression far in excess of Turboquant, and so I think this risk remains remote for now.

Morning fellas. I'm never really active on the short side, but one of the insurers I think it makes sense to take profits on / consider a short position in is American Coastal (ACIC). American Coastal specializes in Commercial Insurance with a focus on Condos, and the market is rapidly deteriorating. Commentary from peers such as American Integrity and Heritage Insurance indicate Commercial market rates are down nearly 20% and that the market is increasingly undisciplined as new entrants chase market share and hammer rates lower.

ACIC is an excellent underwriter and well-managed - I'm not disputing that. However, their significant concentration in the FL Region / their reliance on Commercial and Condo Insurance is a weakness, and I think it is possible EPS drops rapidly from $2 a share to the $1 to $1.50 area. Unlike Homeowners insurance which slowly reprices (clients are less willing to get their home inspected and switch carriers to save a couple hundred dollars) Commercial insurance rates dropping quickly impacts clients rapidly, since their policies can be worth several hundreds of thousands and they will have their broker shop quotes and switch them to the most inexpensive carriers. As a result, I think ACIC's results will inflect lower much more quickly than peers.

Right now, the stock is trading at nearly double Tangible Book Value of $5.57 and 11x the consensus of $1.00 in EPS (the consensus implies hurricane losses, without hurricanes ACIC will probably make $1.50), but I think the lofty premium to Tangible Book and the concentration in a particular line of insurance warrants a lower multiple, perhaps 8x earnings or 1.5x Tangible Book.  I'm short the stock at 0.5% weight at $11.05, looking for downside to $9.50, and will set a stop around $12.50.

Morning gents. Going into Micron earnings, keeping the memory and storage basket capped around 17.5% (previously 20%). I understand the bull case for memory and think Micron will easily beat the $19.25 estimate (probably $21 - $23). Still, I think it is important to understand the bear case. Right now AI bears insist there is no Return on Investment for the hyperscalers, and that as component prices increase, the math becomes increasingly unfavorable.

I understand the argument. Whether you look at Memory or Storage (Western Digital and Seagate), suppliers aren't in a hurry to increase production and surging component prices are placing tremendous strain on the purchasers. Eventually, Cloud Providers are going to need to raise CPU, GPU, and Storage rates, which will not be appreciated by clients.

Despite this, I still think there is Return on Investment for AI, a $5 an hour Nebius instance running data entry or customer services is still vastly underpriced to humans, but we currently seem to be at the point where debt and equity raises and surging component prices are viewed negatively by the market.

Rather than sell positions, I have been reducing exposure by hedging with DRAM, and collaring positions. For example, on Micron you can purchase the July 1000 Put and sell the July 1350 call for about $50. This caps downside to around $50 from current levels, while leaving $300 of upside on the table. If you've been in the stock like I have from the low 200's or 300's, I think this type of protective collar makes a lot of sense, you are eliminating implosion risk (a 20-30% downside move) and leaving decent upside.

Lastly, I think it is important to detatch yourself from your positioning and look at things impartially. It's possible Micron and Memory re-rates to 10x and the cycle lasts several years (as some of the most emphatic bulls on Fintwit believe), but with the stock up 200% YTD a downside move of 10-15% isn't out of the question at all, and a protective collar can help prevent giving back a good portion of your profits.

Morning gents. Decent results out of MOMO. Revenue came in at 2.385 B RMB (2% higher than consensus, I was expecting 2% lower). GAAP earnings ($0.26) and non-GAAP ($0.30) came in much higher than I expected. The company set guidance of 2.45 B to 2.55 B RMB revenue for Q2, the midpoint of which is around 2% lower than the Q2 consensus.

From March 18 to June 3, the company repurchased 3.4 Million shares for $21 Million at an average price of $6.17 a share. Excluding the 45 Million shares held by insiders, there are only about 115 Million shares circulated, so I think the elevated pace of roughly 12% of the float a year is really helpful.

Importantly, International Revenue came in at 597 Million in the quarter, up 44% year over year and now comprises 25% of total revenue. I think that as MOMO "twists" by offsetting declining China results with International growth, it can change its image from Chinese cash cow to an International app portfolio. The company reaffirmed its guidance to hit the 3 Billion RMB milestone in the International segment this year, which means their International revenue is still on track to accelerate roughly 50% this year.

They stated "At this point, our overall view really hasn't changed materially. Depending on how market expansion progresses across different regions, there could still be somewhere around RMB100 million of variation either to the upside or to the downside of that RMB3 billion number."

To summarize, the results came in slightly better than I expected, and while the Q2 guide is slightly lower than consensus, the International growth story remains intact. At < 6x GAAP earnings and way below $6.93 in adjusted cash per share, I think MOMO's International growth prospects and hefty cash balance are not being ascribed much value by the market.

Morning gents. An update on MOMO and Korea.

MOMO is set to report earnings tomorrow. MOMO is considered a melting ice-cube, the China operations (dating app Tantan and livestreaming app Momo) are in a managed decline, and the International operations continue to grow. The analyst estimate of 2.34 B RMD in Revenue and 210 M RMB look a little high to me, I am expecting 2-3% lower than that. The important factors I am paying attention to will be the growth of the International segment (which should help change perception of it being solely a melting ice cube) and capital allocation.

For the period, I am expecting 4 Million shares repurchased in Q1 (they report share repurchases on a trade date period between Mar 18 and June 1, I think this figure will be about 3.6 Million). The share repurchases generate a lot of value given MOMO has Tangible Book of around $9.47 and cash of $6.20 a share, so 4 Million shares repurchased in the quarter at $6 generates $14 Million in Book Value on top of the $24 Million ($0.15 a share) I expect them to make.

The International Segment now comprises about 20% of total revenue, and has grown from 414 M in 2025 Q1, to 442 in Q2, 535 in Q3, and 608 in Q4, a really impressive growth rate. I think the International Segment, if it continues growing at this rate, could really change perception of MOMO from a China decline name, to an International growth name, which could cause a substantial re-rate to perhaps 10x earnings, which would imply 8+ a share.

With all China names (look at what happened to TIGR two weeks ago), I am always concerned about implosion risk, so I try to find ways to protect my position. Looking at the options chain, I think the Janauary 2027 4.74 Puts for $0.15 seem pretty attractive as hedge. Essentially paying just 2.5% of the current price to cap losses to 25%, which makes sense to me since I believe MOMO will be a binary trade, either the fundamentals will really collapse and the stock drops, or MOMO continues hammering the share count while using 100% of its earnings power, and the stock re-rates to $8+.

MOMO is a medium conviction trade for me right now, since all China positions are inherently risky. If MOMO shows continued growth in its International segment while using 100% of  earnings power to repurchase shares, I will happily add to my position after results come out.

Update on $CBL:

The $CBL thesis has largely materialized. The company opportunistically disposed of assets, steadily increased the regular dividend from $0.40 to $0.45 to $0.625 (closer to $0.80 when you include the 4special distributions declared for the rest of this year), same store sales and occupancy stabilized and are inflecting upwards, and most importantly, CBL extended and successfully refinanced the term loan which saw significant interest from CMBS investors. A portion of the refinancing package is interest-only, giving CBL roughly $30 Million in additional cash flow and extra flexibility (a property was released as collateral).

The recent guidance upgrade, refinancing package, and consistently strong operating results have caught the market’s attention. CBL is up roughly 79% (inclusive of dividends) since entry, versus 28% for the broader market, 7% for the real estate benchmark, and peers such as Tanger (2%) and Macerich (18%). By all measures, the company has outperformed significantly, especially in the context of a higher-for-longer environment.
The stock roared past my original optimistic forecast of $42, and currently trades around 6.5x FFO. The valuation is significantly below peers (Tanger and Macerich 14x) and while I could see upside to 7x FFO ($49) or perhaps even 8x (especially if we enter a rates down environment), there are several compelling setups in my portfolio I have been adding to, and I want to be positioned where I see the most favorable risk to reward.

CBL is up 26% YTD, and as you probably saw with Nebius and many other trades, I tend to be wrong when selling into strength. In order to make room for new ideas, I opted for a middle ground approach and reduced two thirds of $CBL position. This isn't me turning bearish on CBL - many positions in the portfolio are up quite a bit YTD, and I am keeping a close eye on any where I think the risk to reward is more balanced, so I can make more room for new entrants that I believe have significant potential.

As expected, memory names finally cooling a bit and I think the move makes sense. On Micron, the most bullish forecasts are for $30 a share in earnings around Q3. With that view in mind, I took my DRAM off yesterday, and I've been selling covered calls on Micron, mostly the September 1300s and 1400s - would love to see another double, but I don't think that is likely. CBL reported excellent Q1 results, with FFO of $1.73 vs $1.50, above the level most were anticipating. The company upgraded guidance from the FFO range of $6.74 - $7.06 to $7.06 to $7.19. Importantly, occupancy edged up to 90.5%, same store tenant sales were up 4.6% year over year, and same store Net Operating Income is up 2.1%, all extremely healthy figures.

CBL was long considered to be in decline, but these recent results, and the significant increase in the dividend, demonstrate this isn't the case. CBL has now neutralized its most pressing "threats". The company fully refinanced the term loan and pushed its maturity to 2031, and looser loan terms are allowing the company to extract cash from previously underperforming properties. CBL has been able to use this increase flexibility to raise the dividend to $0.80 a quarter (a $0.625 regular dividend and a $0.175 special dividend), and now boasts a cash balance greater than $300 Million ($10 a share). With the balance sheet now derisked, and with occupancy and same store sales improving, I think CBL has more room to close the discount to peers (most of whom trade between 12x and 18x FFO). I like to remain grounded in my outlook, but even a small bump to 7x FFO would imply $49 - $50 a share, about 10% upside from the current price. Given the $0.80 quarterly dividend represents a 7% yield, I think CBL is bound to attract additional attention from dividend and real estate investors, as its image continues to improve.

HRTG earnings out. $1.19 vs the $1.53 consensus. Catastrophe and weather losses as well as administrative expenses came in higher than expected. Given the repurchase has been executing around $27, I think it is likely they are more aggressive in the $24 - $25 range which will provide support.

Overall, I was hoping for a beat, and while the numbers were a significant improvement over last year, expectations were high and the quarter is likely to be viewed as disappointing. I'll be paying close attention to the call to see how quickly the management team thinks they can ramp up new business in NY, CA, TX, and will have some orders in the regular session to add tomorrow between $23 and $24 (likely < 6x earnings), but first, I want to see their commentary on the call.

Morning fellas. Wanted to get earnings setups out on IGIC and HRTG, and some thoughts on OPY and SK Square.

IGIC - IGI is set to report earnings tomorrow. I am expecting a softer quarter than consensus, $0.40 - $0.50 vs the $0.71 consensus. IGI is a specialist underwriter and has exposure to political violence, energy, and reinsurance in the Middle East, and I think it is unlikely they were able to totally dodge the impact of the war. The analyst consensus is unchanged since the beginning of the year, and I think they did not update their numbers to reflect recent events. While the impact of the war will dampen Q1 results, I think the war may represent a long-term tailwind for IGIC. Western Businesses are clamoring for political violence coverage, Marine and Marine Cargo rates are through the roof. Should the war come to a conclusion without disarmament, I think these rates are likely to remain high for the next couple of years, if not, the next decade, which will provide a significant tailwind for a specialist like IGI who has a history of deploying capital to generate impressive returns. From the commentary I've read, brokers are still placing coverage and have reported a continual surge in interest, so I believe the Middle Eastern specialists like IGI are likely putting a lot of excess capital to work right now. Nonetheless, I expect IGI was still active on the capital management front, and that they repurchased 500k+ in Q1, vs 300k in 2025 Q4. While global insurance, and reinsurance, rates are in decline, I think IGI will continue to significantly outperform the industry in growth, and underwriting quality, and that sudden shocks like the Middle East ultimately provide a springboard for them to gain more business at attractive rates. If you don't have exposure to IGI, I think a great entry is in the $24 - $25 range, given the company tends to get very aggressive in repurchasing shares in the 23's. Of course, the entry point is dependent on earnings, I will have an update as soon as the numbers are released.

HRTG - Heritage is set to report earnings on Thursday. I am expecting a small beat, $1.75 vs the $1.53 consensus. HRTG's peers, UVE, SLDE, etc, have all handily beat, and I think the $1.53 estimate is within range. What I like about HRTG is its significant national diversification, unlike other 6-8x valued peers (who are heavily concentrated), HRTG has significant business across FL, NY, CA, and now Texas. Similar to commentary from other FL Specialists, I think HRTG will be retaining more risk given their improved balance sheet and attractive underwriting conditions, which should be accretive to 2026 EPS. The analyst consensus seems little changed despite great results from UVE, so I think the setup is prime for a "headline" beat. During the last call, the company mentioned it had repurchased about 100k shares at $27, if the pace continued throughout Q1, I think it might provide a new "anchor" around $27 - $29, which could provide a springboard to $30+. The stock has been bouncing between $25 and $30 for quite some time, but I think a "headline" beat and steady capital allocation will provide room for the next leg up.

I've owned Oppenheimer since 50 in 2024, I think its a long-term outperformer and provides an excellent way to express a view on Investment Banking and Capital Markets at a very inexpensive multiple. If this is a trade you like, I think it makes sense to leg in slowly, it's a volatile name, and it always helps to have extra buying capacity.

Of course, Oppenheimer's Wealth Management Division also benefits heavily from heighted equity values. Over the last two quarters, Oppenheimer has put up $10+ of adjusted earnings a share, its highest on record, demonstrating the scale and operating leverage of its business. I think Oppenheimer's valuation is still sharply below peers, and given Oppenherimer's pace of new hiring, I think the bank is well on its way to expanding from a healthcare and municipal finance specialist, into a broader investment bank which should help it rerate. I wouldn't pay too much attention to the legal settlement and the OAR compensation expense, the legal settlement is one time in nature, and the OAR charge is simply a matter of the stock increasing in value. I view compensation tied to the stock price as much more preferable than bloated RSU compensation expense that is granted regardless of performance.

IESC - $5.44 GAAP EPS and $4.16 adjusted EPS. IES came in close to the one analyst estimate. Several names in the portfolio reported earnings: Samsung Electronics, OSB Group, Vistance Networks, Ategrity Specialty Insurance, Itafos

Samsung: EPS of 8,000 vs 6,100 consensus, although with Hynix results already reported, this beat wasn't a surprise. DRAM average selling price was up 90%, NAND was up 90% as well. Importantly, the company stated demand was surging from clients who wanted to pull forward orders, and that the supply demand gap is getting wider into 2027 which is great news for pricing. Overall an excellent quarter, but came in right as everyone expected given the news out of hyperscalers and Hynix's report earlier in the month. The stock is currently trading around 6x forward earnings, but I like the preferred shares a bit more at 4x earnings.

OSB Group: OSB released a strong Q1 update. The loan book is growing slightly faster than consensus, Net Interest Margin is in line, and the company is planning on a 5% dividend increase. Not much has changed, but I think the re-assuring update has calmed markets.

Vistance: Another quarter of excellent capital management. After paying a massive $10 dividend (return of capital) just a few days ago, Vistance has sold another gem, it's Ruckus Wifi division, to Belden for $1.85 Billion. The company plans to pay out the proceeds via a special dividend no later than 60 days after the transaction closes. After the sale closes, Vistance will be just a small shell of its former self with its Aurora Networks division, but the company will likely take out a bit of debt and financial engineer the balance sheet to generate even more value for shareholders. Until then, happy to stay long, Vistance is really a flag bearer for excellent capital allocation, rather than run the company into the ground the management team wisely said "ok, let's wind things down" and the sale of Ruckus to Belden at a nice premium reflects how they are doing everything to maximize value for the shareholders.

Ategrity Specialty: ASIC is down on what I thought was a good quarter. The bears assert much of the quarter's "beat" was contributed by net investment income, $8 Million last year vs $12 Million this year, but I think 85% year over year growth in Underwriting Income and 22% in top-line growth is also impressive. Ategrity's niche of catering to small businesses via E&S lines continues to handily outperform broader E&S industry growth, and even though E&S as a whole is decelerating sharply, I think Ategrity will continue to grow 10-20% faster than peers. The stock is down on extremely thin volume, and I added to my position in the low 19s. The only thing that disappointed me was the lack of progress on the repurchase program this quarter, but given they are operating at a Return on Equity of 16% and rapidly growing, I don't fault them for retaining capital. What I like about Ategrity is that they have a niche, are outgrowing the industry significantly, have an extremely aligned owner (Stuart Zimmer owns 80%), continue to post disciplined underwriting profits, and trade at a sub-industry multiple (currently around 10x). I added to my position today, I think eventually Ategrity will trade at 12-14x, implying the mid to high 20s.

Itafos - Itafos was the only name of the 5 that had a "disappointing" quarter, but I don't think the news was really a surprise and the management team indicating this at the recent investor webinar. Itafos's fertilizer products are sold on an offtake agreement at a 90 day rolling price, while its input costs "sulphuric acid" reprice instantly. What this means is that in March, Itafos was hurt by rapidly soaring Sulphuric acid prices, but saw almost zero benefit from rising global fertilizer prices. This effect will be partially reversed in Q2 as the 90 day average begins reflecting post war prices by the beginning of May, and Q2 results should be much improved. Eventually, when the war ends, Itafos will experience bumper results as input costs (sulphuric acid) plummet, but the company is still able to sell fertilizer at an elevated 3 month average price. I think Itafos management is extremely competent, and that this quarter was simply the unfortunate result of having an input price that moves along with spot, and an output price that is a three month rolling average.

The company itself tried to highlight this in the report: "Furthermore, due to the pricing mechanism of our long-term MAP offtake contract (three-month historical average prices), the full benefit of higher product prices were not fully reflected in our Q1 sales revenues. We therefore expect our revenues to increase on a per unit basis in the coming quarter." I think the management team, via this line, is trying to spell it out that Q1 was really just a result of a difference between how inputs and outputs repriced. Q2 should be much better, and I added to my position near $3, below current Tangible Book Value of $3.15. Obviously, don't want to go too heavy for a Canadian mining name, but Itafos has a place as one of the only physical assets I own in my portfolio. I think the company is extremely well run, and that it will return to a 8-10 cents a share earnings pace later in the year as input and output costs normalize.

Earnings Review and Setups: Hynix, CUBI, FIX, OPY

Hynix: Hynix reported revenue of 52.5 T (vs 50.8 T consensus) and operating income of 37.6 T vs 36 T consensus. The earnings per share figure is not directly applicable since it includes Hynix's gain on its Kioxia stake. The stock had minimal reaction, most of these forecasts were raised significantly in the days preceding earnings, and the whisper number for a larger beat didn't materialize. DRAM ASP (average selling price) was up 60% YOY, and NAND up 70% YOY, but volume was down. The company explained this was due to changes in production, and I think this provides them room to improve next quarter.

Importantly, an analyst asked about Spot DRAM prices, and the management team told everyone it shouldn't be viewed as indicative at all:

"Now we understand that there are various interpretations in the market regarding the recent spot price movement. So let me share with you the company's perspective. Now first of all, the spot market itself takes up a very small part of the overall DRAM market. And the types and volume of products that are traded there differ considerably from our business. So we can't really view these changes in the spot market as reflective of the overall market. On one hand, we see that the memory demand from our major customers is increasing across the board, including HBM, server DRAM, and eSSD. On the other hand, for the suppliers, the reality is that the suppliers find it hard-pressed to increase supply in the short-term."

The company also flagged its 100 Trillion cash balance, and stated further shareholder return programs were under consideration. My guess is that prior to the listing of the ADR, Hynix commences a buyback, so as to avoid diluting existing shareholders. I still like Hynix and memory names, but I think after a 30% run up in the recent month, it makes sense to pause a potential entry and wait to see how the market digests these results.

CUBI: Customers Bank reports earnings tonight. The estimate of 1.89 seems within reach, although I think Customers might come in slightly below that range. What I am more focused on, and what I think most investors are focused on, is credit quality. Customers has a growing NDFI Portfolio, in which they lend to VC Funds, PE Funds, and occasionally, Business Development Corporations. Customers has had impeccable credit quality since the inception of this segment, part of the reason for this is due to their "Wholistic Banking" approach. Unlike other banks who simply focus on lending, Customers demands these clients make Customers their primary bank. This gives CUBI exceptional visibility into the health of their clients: they can view cash flow, operating account balances, etc, and use the data to make informed lending decisions. Naturally, there has been a lot of concern about anything adjacent to Private Credit over the last couple of months, and I think those concerns alone were what pummeled the stock from 82 to 65, before its recent recovery.

I'm looking to see CUBI steadily grow its organic deposits via the new banking teams it has poached over the last couple of years, stable credit quality, and flat balances across its proprietary CUBIX network, a 24/7 internal stablecoin that allows crypto trading participants to move USD to each other. CUBIX is an entirely Institutional offering, participants are all Customers Bank clients, and it is used in lieu of stablecoins, to ensure no theft occurs (it is a closed loop network, so only known participants can send to each other eliminating the possibility of a hack). When crypto volumes rise, the balances on CUBIX tend to rise as well, this quarter I am expecting balances to remain flat or slightly down despite the elevated activity, however.

Ultimately, if they can come in 1.80 or above with stable credit quality I will be pleased. I think the setup here is perfectly balanced, the stock has run up significantly, but it is also a high quality bank and I believe they will continue to outperform the industry. Customers trades < 10x earnings in contrast to the industry at 12x, over time I expect the valuation gap to narrow.

OPY: Oppenheimer never announces the earnings date, but I believe they will report tomorrow. The setup for the quarter is unusual: earnings should be negatively impacted by $2 a share due to an increase in the value of the OARs (Appreciation Rights granted to employees, cash settled call options), and depressed market valuations at the end of Q1 (the market has rallied 9% since March 31).

Given how large the impact of the OARs will be, I expect the company will reference the impact in the release, enabling us to back the charge out, and figure out what the core performance of the business is. Despite the $2 headwind, I think Oppenheimer is still on track for $2 a share in earnings, and would be very surprised, and impressed, to see that figure higher. Trading revenues and brokerage commissions should positively impact Q1, and subsequent to Q1, we've seen a surge in biotech equity raises, which should significantly benefit Oppenheimer's capital markets profits in Q2. I think it is important to be aware of the negative impact of the OARs on earnings per share. Oppenheimer's stock price was unmoved in Q4, so record earnings of $6.51 were entirely unimpacted. That isn't the same for this quarter, but ultimately I am not that concerned about the impact of the OARs. I think a variable compensation program where employee bonuses are tied to the share performance serves as excellent alignment in an investment banking context, it keeps overhead low and significantly motivates employees. Aside from the negative impact of the OARs on earnings, I think the setup for Oppenheimer in 2026 is still excellent, in the last couple of days there has been a surge in activity: the IPO of Odyssey Therapeutics, a secondary from Trevi, Target Hospitality, and Spruce Biosciences. If activity can sustain at this level, I think Oppenheimer has the chance to report three consecutive quarters of profitability from the Capital Markets division, which will transform perception of the company from a Wealth Manager with a cash incinerating Capital Markets division, to a full fledged investment bank with a strong position in biotech and municipal finance.

Afternoon fellas. Just a quick note on risk, I see a lot of people opining that shorting stuff like CAR at these valuations is free money. I myself was short one share, which I closed for a nasty 200 dollar loss. I think it is absolutely not worth the risk to even consider shorting these types of names.

The top two holders of CAR, SRS and Pentwater, own 25 Million shares out of 35 Million, roughly 70%. They have further exposure to 12 Million Total Return Swaps (products issued by banks that replicate the performance of ownership). Simply put, they have economic exposure greater than all shares outstanding. The Total Return Swaps are hedged by the banks by either purchasing the underlying, or pairing against other clients who are bearish (who are likely feeling pressure to close out). 

Unlike most squeezes where retail goes after hedge funds, this appears to be highly unique: it's a fund versus fund fight.

Aside from CAR's 5 Million at the market program, there have been no filings from SRS and Pentwater, indicating they want to hold out and let the pain continue. The risk of shorting these names cannot be overstated. Unlike buying value names at reasonable multiple where you can only lose your initial investment, something like CAR could cause losses significantly in excess of your capital. Even something that seems far-fetched, like selling deep out of the money calls, could rapidly spiral into a dangerous position.

Sometimes you just have to say "it isn't worth the risk" - I would certainly not have any negative exposure to CAR while these antics continue, no matter what valuation it is trading at.

Morning fellas. Lot of chatter on the Turboquant paper from Google. For those of you who aren't familiar, AI models consume a lot of VRAM (Video Random Access Memory) on GPUs. One part is the model (weights) itself, another part is KV cache, this is the context window where people chat, attach files, images, etc. What Google figured out is they could compress the context window by up to 8x with minimal accuracy loss, meaning that conversations consume way less VRAM. In theory, this means users could input way more data (coding, image editing) without running into the context window. For anyone who has used Deepresearch or NotebookLM, you've likely run into this - the services limit Context Windows since Context Windows use extreme amounts of RAM and they simply can't accommodate more than a few 50 page PDFs.

The reaction to Turboquant seems to be two-sided. On one hand, the knee-jerk reaction from the bears is "to sell memory". It is easy to see where they are coming from, their argument is that because the context window can be compacted, GPU efficiency roars, and thus less memory and gpus are needed to handle the current workload. On the other hand, bulls are citing "Jevons Paradox", that  improved efficiency and lower costs actually increases demand because something is more economically effective.

Right now, I see both sides a bit. I don't think this will materially impact the memory market unless Nvidia comes out and says "ok, because of this our chips can use way less memory" now. More efficient inference and larger context windows should make AI even more effective, and it also appears this technology has already existed for a year and Chinese names like Deepseek have reported something similar (although with much more accuracy loss). On the other hand, judging from the reaction on Twitter, the bulls seem extremely defensive and bitter.

Just a little rant here - I think AI is massively deflationary for the services category. Most of inflation over the last 5 years has been services, not goods, and with AI bringing the software train to a brutal halt, think we now have room for a steeper yield curve (short-term rates are cut, long-term rates remain steady).

Bodes well for banks, insurance, value names, maybe helps tech a bit but I am not so sure. I have been playing with Claude Code and Codex and I encourage you to as well, it's like having a software developer in your pocket. Most of corporate America is rife with ridiculously overpaid people, it's essentially "daycare" when you watch those "day in a life videos". The software names in particular have raised prices 5% - 10% a year with no justification, and everyone just went along with it.

Now that AI is cloning much of this software in a matter of minutes at near zero cost, people are really changing the way they value Software. Terminal values are evaporating, and frankly, I think the guys who are going to be left holding the bag are BDCs and Direct Lending funds, who have provided financing to high leverage software names. The sector is already in the toilet, but to expand on the most recent article, a few names above book value (who have traditionally taken small equity stakes in many of the companies they lend to) such as HTGC, TRIN, MAIN, stand out.

It doesn't take a genius to realize the value of these high leverage SOFR + 5.00% software loans aren't worth 100, they are likely down to 95 or 90 or possible even worse! Several BDCs are taking write downs, such as GBDC, and have to cut the dividend as they realize 15% payouts are impossible with the losses they are taking.
The saddest thing about the sector is many of these names prey on elderly investors and wealth management firms who do not understand what they own, but happily tell their clients about "income". Over the next 3-5 years I anticipate most of these funds will provide substandard returns, or perhaps even losses, as "one time" write downs outweigh "investment income". I think it's worth adding the names to your watchlist to keep an eye on the health of the sector.

As for memory and storage names, I am not concerned.

I think everyone is underestimating how rapid the transformation will be, and the calls for a "bubble" in names like Hynix and Samsung are very misplaced. Names like Micron and Hynix are barely upping capital expenditures, and are going to enjoy record high margins.

My point is, names like Hynix are trading 5-6x surge earnings, and probably 10x earnings once things cool down.

MBIN - Great results, asset quality with a big improvement, EPS $1.28 vs $0.94, fresh $100 Million share repurchase program announced. WSBF - Very strong quarter at $0.44. No estimates, but I am pleased with the results. Net Interest Income continues to grow steadily, and the mortgage segment posted the strongest results in years. The company still trades at a nearly $2 discount to book, and repurchased another 140,000 shares to take advantage of this. I think the stock is well on its way to make $2 a share this year, which means it is currently trading at just 8.5x earnings, a very compelling valuation given the upwards optionality of the mortgage underwriting segment. Ultimately, I think the mortgage segment is worth a significant premium to book, and that WSBF will one day be acquired by someone looking to grow their own mortgage business. While WSBF's mortgage segment is what most people care about, Net Interest Income has grown from 13.7 Million in Q2, to 14.7 Million in Q3, to 15.5 Million in Q4. This steady improvement as a result of declining deposit costs will drive steady improvements regardless of whether mortgage income increases. WSBF already has a tailwind from this, plus the upwards optionality of the mortgage business kicking into overdrive when people begin refinancing. An excellent setup, even after the recent rally, in my opinion.

The repurchase programs for all three offer nice setups, either the names drift upwards as a result of heavy demand for the stock, or if they decline, more shares are taken out at attractive valuations, ultimately boosting long-term value and growing earnings per share. MBIN has relatively high short interest as people bet against their credit quality, I think the good report and a rebuttal of the credit quality theme will give it the most upside out of the three, but I like all of them. At a discount to book (industry trades at 1.2x - 1.5x Tangible Book Value) and at 7 - 8.5x earnings (industry trades at 11 - 14x), I think they have much more upside than peers.

You won't get a spectacular return, but I think they are stable, outperforming names, and if you have an interest in regional banks they are worth looking into.

The Supreme Court has indicated a decision on tariffs may come out as soon as tomorrow. While the "Tariff Removal" basket I posted in November is up almost 60%, I legged back into the names (I already own CBL separately). It's a speculative bet and honestly I think many names are already "priced in" such as Sonos and GCT, but I think there might be a knee-jerk reaction if a headline comes out tomorrow. The first 8 names from the previous basket are highly sensitive, and the additional names (SONO, W, GAP, AXL, UAA, NKE, ANF, FND, MAT) also have significant exposure to tariffs.

I'm not a litigation expert, but I have a feeling the court rules against President Trump. He is likely losing the 3 Democrat aligned votes (Sotomayor, Kagan, Ketanji Brown),  Gorsuch has expressed libertarian tendencies, Barrett dislikes him, and Thomas and seem to be originalist interpreters of laws, and it seems like the law does not allow the current interpretation. I think the base case is that tariffs are ruled invalid, and I also think Trump will be hesitant to meltdown and institute Sectoral Tariffs on clothing, toys, fashion (which comprise most of this basket). Especially in a midterm year.

If a positive bump does occur, I will be quick to lock in some profit on the basket (aside from CBL), as it is almost certain we get a essay-esque tweet about how he isn't finished yet, but given the extremely high short interest in the fashion components (DBI, COLM, UAA), I think people will be quick to close out these names, many of whom are still down 40-50% from their March 2025 pre-tariff highs. A removal of tariffs shouldn't impact AXL, LEA, and GCT who already suffer from sectoral tariffs related to Autoparts and Furniture, but I think they may trade up in sympathy and so I included them in the list.

Wish I had just held the basket from the very beginning, but I think these names worth keeping an eye on tomorrow if a decision comes out, even if you want a wait-and-see approach. If the court somehow rules the tariffs are valid, the market likely has a very nasty reaction. Without the overhang of tariffs though, I think Trump can still take a win with his existing Sectoral Tariffs, and the tailwind to inflation should allow him to appoint someone that "runs it hot".
