Time Sensitive Odd Lot Opportunity - Potential $179 One Day Profit

Good Morning. A short term odd lot trade just popped up.

Tile Shop Holdings (TTSH) on Friday announced it will conduct a 1 for 3,000 reverse stock split, followed immediately by a 3,000 for 1 split, effective after market close today. The transaction is designed to cash out stockholders owning fewer than 3,000 shares, since the company wants to delist.

According to the press release, holders of 2,999 shares or fewer prior to the close of business today (4 PM), will receive $6.60 in cash per share.

With the stock trading at $6.54 an odd-lot arbitrage opportunity is present. You can purchase up to 2,999 shares, and have them cashed out for a 6 cent profit ($179). The cash might not be paid out tomorrow, but should be received in short order.

These tenders can aggregate your position across social security number, not account, so I wouldn't steer clear of doing 2,999 across multiple accounts. If they detect you own greater than 3,000 shares the corporate action will not apply and you'll be stuck owning the shares, as a result the MAXIMUM you can purchase is 2,999 shares in one account.
Keep this trade on the down low, even at 6.56 or 6.57 (3 cents profit is $90), it might be worth your time. Obviously you can't pay more than 6.60 or you'd lose money. This isn't risk free, it is possible the corporate action is canceled, but I think that is highly unlikely given the transaction was approved by 80% of the shareholders and is scheduled to go through today. Additionally, you can enter at a smaller size, 2,999 shares is simply the maximum you can own and remain eligible.

IGIC reports today.

There are a few tailwinds, primarily the dollar strengthening 2%, but there are also a few unknowns, namely catastrophe losses related to Typhoon Ragasa.

Gross and net written premiums should decline relative to Q2 because IGI is stepping away from unprofitable long-tail professional lines business in Europe, and reinsurance activity is lower. While some may fret over a lower top line, I think this illustrates why IGI is an above average insurer. The allure of smaller underwriters is that they pursue the highest risk adjusted opportunities and reduce exposure to undperforming lines unlike the larger names. During the last call, IGI indicated premiums would be down as they step away from unprofitable professional lines in Europe.

The GBP has weakened further from 1.34 to 1.30, but this tailwind will kick in during Q4 and not Q3. I think share repurchases will be much lower than last quarter's 1 Million, something around 100,000. They historically don't repurchase many shares in Q3 since wind events can impact results.

It's difficult to forecast earnings, since IGI is a smaller insurer and catastrophes like the California wildfires or Typhoons can heavily impact results. I'm more concerned about their outlook for 2026 and if IGI can continue to pursue excellent risk adjusted opportunities. The analyst estimate of 83 cents seems very high to me, I think he is adjusting for FX. I am looking for a much lower figure.

Despite IGI's small size and the disadvantage of having natural disasters impact results given the smaller book of business, I think IGI's size is actually its best asset, since it is one of the only small insurers with the scale to compete globally, but is still nimble and conservative enough to walk away from underperforming areas as markets continue to shift.

Good luck to all. I still like IGI, and despite  industry headwinds and sentiment being heavily downtrodden across insurance, I think IGI has an opportunity to continue outperforming the industry.

Wanted to do a brief primer on what's going on within banking and insurance.

Regional banks and private credit are getting slammed due to recent events: the collapse of Tri Color, First Brands, and the loss provisions taken by Zions due to fraud. For years, private credit and increasingly creative financing techniques like "factoring" were hailed as the next big thing. Due to massive (likely fraud) uncovered at Tri Color and First Brands, as well as Zions Bank taking a sizeable $50 Million loss provision today in connection with two loans (likely also fraud related), people are heading for the exists and are questioning the validity of marks on private vehicles and are asking "is this more widespread".

Liquidity within small caps today is limited. Program sellers are indiscriminately selling banks, many of whom have little to no exposure to recent events. One of the banks I like is OP Bancorp (OPBK), a California bank. Given the limited size of their portfolio and footprin
t, I think it's unlikely they were a "large" enough player to be associated with Tri Color, First Brands, or Cantor Group V (which had massive revolving lines of credit that were extended by Western Alliance and Zions, among other large plauers). They have an extremely liability sensitive balance sheet (1.5 Billion in rate sensitive liabilities, 1.2 Billion in rate sensitive assets), so lower rates provides an immense tailwind. The bank is trading at $13, roughly 7x my 2026 EPS estimate of $1.88, and at just 0.81x 2025 Tangible Book Value of $15.26.

Another name I nibbling at is Oppenheimer (OPY). Oppenheimer is getting slapped in connection with Jefferies and the wider investment bank peer group, but there is a huge difference between the way they operate. Oppenheimer has a minimal risk balance sheet, and its primary revenue sources are from its wealth management advisory segment, and to a lesser extent, capital markets. It has no significant connections to private credit.

On a day like today, all the investment banks and private credit firms are getting split open. Oppenheimer is trading slightly below Tangible Book Value of $68.25, and roughly 9x Earnings of $7.71, 8x my 2026 Estimate of $8.50.

At a slight discount to Tangible Book, I nibbled at both today. We could go back to 2023 when everything traded at 0.6-0.7x book due to sheer panic, but I don't think that will happen.

Within insurance, the entire sector is falling apart as the flag bearers, Progressive and many insurance brokers get totally slammed on  earnings. Progressive had a soft Q3, and took a large charge because they actually made too much in Florida and had to return their profits to policyholders. With Progressive down 10% in roughly two days, and Berkshire down 10% since Buffett's resignation, sentiment is awful. Frankly, I think a few names like AIG and TRV are still overvalued, but there is a sizeable chunk of large cap investors who like to purchase them at 10x forward earnings, and so it's difficult to be bearish. I think there are a few pockets of opportunity on the long side, Heritage (6x forward), and International General Insurance (7.5x forward) have been swinging wildly on minimal volume. Both of them have vastly different exposure from AIG, Travelers, Progressive, but are trading in sympathy.

I think a good chunk of the move in smaller regional banks and insurers is due to the blackout window. Since we are right in the middle of earnings season, pretty much no one is allowed to repurchase shares and provide some liquidity within the stock.

Today is the worst day in regional banks since last October (excluding two days in April), so I wouldn't be surprised to see some crazy moves into the closer. Over the long run, though, I think OPY, OPBK, IGIC have vastly different exposures as compared to the names getting killed today, and at 7x earnings on pretty much all of them, they will outperform over the long rub.

I also still have Customers (CUBI), but given their new niche is filling the void of SVB by courting Private Equity and Venture Capital (via capital call loans and fund finance), I'd be surprised if they catch a bid until earnings next Thursday. Hopefully they can set the record straight then an assuage fears after reporting earnings. I think a lot of banks may start pre-releasing earnings after hours to try and calm investors.

nt development. St Georges stock is going ballistic, and so this benefits Itafos since they are the second largest holder of St Georges (no one seems to remember this since when the initial transaction took place, SGQ was tiny).

Gotta be gentle on this one, a name I have been adding to almost every day in Japan is 9478, SE Holdings and Incubations. It's a tiny company with a market cap of just 40 Million USD, but the gem of the company isn't the publishing business, but rather the 58 Million Securities Portfolio and the 19 Million cash balance.
The securities portfolio flies under the radar because it's buy and hold. Unrealized gains on the stock positions don't show up unless they are closed out, which the company never does. With the Nikkei up 12% since June, the HSI 11%, and the S&P 500 8.7%, it's likely the securities portfolio appreciated significantly, and that Tangible Book Value per share is much higher than last reported figure of 571 Yen per share (the stock is at just 360).

What I like most about 9478 is the capital management, unlike most value traps they repurchase a bunch of shares. Since the end of Q2, the fully expended their buyback of 267,900 shares at 373 (about 2.5% of the float), and I expect a fresh buyback to be announced after the next earnings report.
This is extremely deep value investing, and I think it works out long term with the current 60% upside to Net Assets. The company has grown tangible book value by 16% over the last year from 492 to 571 Yen per share, and I think these positive results will continue.

In Japan, flashing a large buy or sell order reduces the chance of a fill, so I've been fishing for small amounts each day, 500 or 1000 shares, to add to my position below the 373 average repurchase price they paid in the quarter.

A small cap I've been adding to recently is Oppenheimer. I wrote it up a while ago at 50 and again at 66, currently trading at 70, just a tad above the Tangible Book Value of 68 (book value of 86). Oppenheimer is an investment bank, but its real gem is the wealth management division, which manages 52 Billion, along with an additional 80 Billion in retail brokerage money. What I like about Oppenheimer is the predictable nature of the wealth management division, and the fee-based nature of the advisory investment bank. Oppenheimer doesn't take risk, unlike a bank or insurer who can blow up, Oppenheimer's income stream is substantially de-risked. In the past four quarters, OPY made 7.71, which puts it around 9x earnings, but the earnings haven't told the full picture due to employee stock options, which have heavily impacted earnings.

Oppenheimer has 2.6 Million Oppenheimer Appreciation Rights (OARs), cash settled incentive compensation for employees that pays out as the stock appreciates. If the stock goes up 6 bucks, pre-tax compensation expense increases by 15 Million.

Obviously, as Oppenheimer has increased from 50 to 70 over the past year, expenses associated with the OARs increased.

In Q3 2025, the stock rose from 65 to 73, which will provide an additional $14 Million hit (roughly $1.30 a share). Nonetheless, capital markets and deal making were red hot in Q3, and rising markets not only boost Oppenheimer's capital markets segment, they boost overall AUM and management fees. I think Oppenheimer trades at a massive discount to peers given its impressive turnaround since 2022, and I think the setup gets attractive when it trades close to Tangible Book Value ($68).

It may seem like dead money, but over the last 10 years OPY has put up an annualized 17.79%, 3 points above SPY at 14.38%, and significant outperformance over XLF at 12.90%. Whenever it trades close to Tangible Book value, I think it is worth a look.
